content: The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends specific viral load (VL) thresholds to differentiate between treatment failure and undetectable viral levels. A viral load greater than 1,000 copies/mL indicates treatment failure, while a viral load of 50 copies/mL or less is considered undetectable. Updates have been made to clarify the numerator in calculations, but the method of calculating the indicator and its purpose remain unchanged. On page 75, Figure 3 has been replaced with a corrected version. On page 309, line 23, the term HIV status (positive, negative) has been updated to HIV status (positive, negative, unknown status). The numerator should be based on the best available data sources, including direct estimates from HIV case surveillance systems. These systems should report the number of people living with HIV who have been diagnosed and are still alive. Only confirmed HIV diagnoses should be included, and mechanisms must be in place to avoid duplicate reporting of individuals across multiple facilities. Modeled estimates may also be used, depending on the availability of country-specific data. For countries with robust case surveillance and vital registration systems, the number of people aware of their HIV status can be derived using the Case Surveillance and Vital Registration (CSAVR) fitting tool within the Spectrum AIDS Impact Module (AIM). For the denominator, estimation models such as Spectrum AIM are the preferred source for determining the number of people living with HIV. When estimating the number of children (ages 0–14) who know their HIV status in countries relying on modeled estimates based on household survey data, additional program data may be required. This is because household surveys often focus on respondents of reproductive age. A separate estimate for children may need to be constructed to produce an overall estimate across all age groups. On page 386, lines 23–24, the description of probable routes of HIV transmission has been updated. The revised list includes heterosexual sex, sex between men, unprotected intercourse during sex work, injecting drug use with unsterile equipment, nosocomial transmission, vertical transmission, and other routes. On page 386, lines 26–27, the definition of key populations has been expanded. It now includes men who have sex with men, people living in prisons and other closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender and gender-diverse individuals, as well as adolescent girls and young women. These corrections have been incorporated into the electronic file.
